Design report · rev A5 · 2026-09-06

MDX-1 simultaneous multi-frequency + pulse-induction metal detector

A complete, ERC-checked KiCad schematic and an initial 4-layer PCB for a detector built on the same architecture as current high-end simultaneous multi-frequency detectors, with a receive chain and transmit engine specified beyond what commercial units publish: five simultaneous frequencies from a single optimised 3-level waveform, a 24-bit 512 kSPS coherent receiver with no automatic gain, a second 24-bit channel digitising the transmit current, and a 100 V bipolar pulse-induction mode on the same H-bridge.

What was delivered, and what can honestly be claimed

Design and production tools. The KiCad files are the source of truth for the schematic and boards; fab_jlc.py produces the fabrication package from the board, tx_waveform_opt.py is the transmit-waveform optimiser, and coil_calc.py computes the coil electromagnetics.

Claims, stated plainly

  • Verified: the schematic loads in KiCad 10, every one of the 1104 pin connections matches the design intent (independent netlist comparison), and ERC is clean (0 errors, 0 warnings). Every rail capacitor is drawn wired to the pin it decouples and the PCB builder places it beside that pin, so layout is unambiguous.
  • Specified beyond typical commercial units on paper: receiver resolution and dynamic range, transmit flexibility, and the simultaneous 24-bit transmit-current reference. Section 2 details the engine.
  • Not claimed: that a first build will out-detect a mature commercial detector in the field. Detector performance is decided by firmware (ground tracking, discrimination, noise cancel) and coil quality as much as by electronics, and neither has been built or tested. The hardware removes the usual limits; the firmware plan in section 6 describes how to use that headroom.
  • Rev A5 changes: the detector can run without the UI board at all (phone app + headphones or Bluetooth headphones + a power button): link pin 8 became UI_DET (grounded on the UI board, pulled up on the main board, read at boot), and the main board gained its own POWER button and status LED in parallel with the UI board's. Firmware option MDX_UI_BOARD = 0 / 1 / 2 (headless build, always fitted, auto-detect).
  • Rev A4 changes: the MCU's fourteen VDD pins are tied to the +3V3 plane with one 4.7 µF and one 100 nF at the package (the per-pin capacitors were removed); the display, six-key pad, pinpoint trigger, power key, LEDs and front-light LED move to a separate 82 × 60 mm two-layer UI board linked by a 20-way 0.5 mm FFC, with the front-light driver, IMU, audio and radios staying on the main board.
  • Review before fabrication: pinouts come from KiCad's verified library symbols, but the passive values, regulator feedback networks and connector choices are my design and need a normal engineering review. The PCB is placed and routed; run DRC for your fabricator before ordering.
2

The target architecture and MDX-1's engine

Published specifications, teardown reports and the multi-frequency detector patent literature converge on one architecture for high-end VLF detectors: a rectangular (switched) transmit waveform whose Fourier lines supply several frequencies at once, synchronous demodulation of each line, and ground rejection by linear combinations across frequencies. Gold machines use pulse induction with constant-current or bipolar transmit. MDX-1 implements both in one set of electronics.

The two published numbers that measure "engine" capability directly are the transmit frequency set and the transmit level; everything else a detector advertises (recovery speed, target-ID stability, salt handling, iron bias) is firmware operating on the demodulated signals. MDX-1's receive and transmit engine is specified so that none of those functions is limited by analog headroom, timing jitter or processor throughput:

  • Five simultaneous frequencies — 5, 10, 15, 20 and 40 kHz (harmonics 1, 2, 3, 4, 8 of 5.12 kHz) from a single optimised 3-level look-up-table waveform with equal line amplitudes and zero DC.
  • Programmable transmit rail, 7.9–29.8 V by DAC injection into the boost feedback, so transmit level is a menu setting; the frequency set is firmware-defined and the receiver is wideband (4–45 kHz).
  • Two 24-bit 512 kSPS channels — one digitises the receive coil, the second digitises the transmit current for exact VRX/ITX normalisation. Fixed gain, no AGC or blanking; dynamic range comes from the converter, not gain switching.
  • 100 V bipolar pulse induction on the same H-bridge, with zero-voltage freewheel hold and constant-current regulation from the transmit-current channel; pulse rate, reversal amplitude, hold length and sample windows are all firmware parameters.
3

Architecture

Coherent timing, one crystal

A 16.384 MHz crystal drives the MCU PLL (458.752 MHz core), the ADC master clocks (MCO2 = 16.384 MHz, OSR 32 → 512 kSPS) and TIM1 (229.376 MHz) that generates the transmit waveform. One transmit period is 195.3125 µs = exactly 100 ADC samples = 44,800 timer ticks. Demodulation is an exact 100-point DFT per period, so there is no spectral leakage between the five lines and no phase drift between transmit and receive.

Two 24-bit channels, not one

A published multi-frequency signal-processing technique normalises the receive signal by a reference proportional to transmit current (S = VRX/VREF). MDX-1 digitises that reference with an identical converter and filter path, so the complex ratio is exact in magnitude and phase at every line, and rail sag, coil heating and inductance change with soil permeability drop out of the target and ground vectors before any balancing is done.

4

Transmit: five equal lines from one 3-level waveform

Rectangular transmit is the established approach in the multi-frequency detector patents, and it is the right choice: a class-D bridge is efficient, and the Fourier lines of a periodic 3-level waveform can be put where the receiver wants them. Instead of mixing two square waves (which yields geometrically spaced lines), the MDX-1 waveform is an 80-slot look-up table per 195.3 µs period, found by simulated annealing to give equal voltage amplitude at harmonics 1, 2, 3, 4 and 8 of 5.12 kHz with zero DC.

10.24 kHz0.2245.38 V245 mA
15.36 kHz0.2255.41 V164 mA
20.48 kHz0.2265.42 V124 mA
40.96 kHz0.2265.42 V63 mA

Design consequences

  • At 12 V the coil draws 0.42 A rms and 0.81 A peak, dissipating 0.10 W in the winding. The rail is programmable from 7.9 V to 29.8 V by DAC injection into the LT3757 feedback node, so transmit level is a menu setting; at 30 V the current lines scale 2.5×, which is the "more power" lever that high-end units advertise, without changing anything else.
  • Equal voltage lines mean equal induced target EMF at every frequency (target EMF ∝ ω·I ∝ V for an inductive load), which is what keeps target ID consistent from 5 to 41 kHz.
  • The minimum feature is one 2.44 µs slot; the 150 V MOSFETs with 4.7 Ω gate resistors switch in about 40 ns, and TIM1 dead time is 100 ns, so the waveform is reproduced without distortion.
  • Other frequency sets (an alternative 4/8/14/24/40 kHz, or a single 7.8 kHz for salt, or a 40/80 kHz pair for small gold) are just different tables; the receiver and both ADCs are wideband.

Receive: low noise, no gain switching, 110 dB of headroom

Per input, 41 kHz (5 kHz)2.0 (1.5)

In a 10 Hz detection bandwidth that is 9 nV rms referred to the coil. Field noise (EMI, ground) will dominate by orders of magnitude; the point is that the electronics never set the floor.

Why there is no automatic gain

Every high-end detector reconciles a µV target signal with a ground signal that can be a thousand times larger using variable gain, blanking or careful nulling. The MDX-1 front end has a fixed gain of 20 into a 24-bit converter with about 110 dB signal-to-noise at 512 kSPS. Full scale at the ADC corresponds to ±125 mV at the coil; the LSB corresponds to 15 nV. A residual coil null of 20 mV and a very mineralised ground response leave more than 80 dB above the noise floor for the target, which is why the same hardware can serve salt beaches, hot rocks and PI mode without a mode switch in the analog path.

  • The two OPA1612 halves form the classic two-amplifier instrumentation stage: 1 kΩ feedback each, one 105 Ω gain resistor, so common-mode pickup on the coil cable is passed at unity and subtracted by the THS4551.
  • Coil inputs are AC-coupled and biased to VOCM (1.65 V) so the whole chain sits at the ADC's common-mode; the BAS416 clamps also reference VOCM and protect the preamp during PI flyback, with recovery in about 2 µs.
  • THS4551 fully-differential drivers with a 240 kHz RC keep the wideband FIR's transition band clean; both channels are identical so the group delay cancels in the ratio.
6

Signal processing plan (firmware)

Everything below runs on the 480 MHz Cortex-M7 in double precision. The budget per transmit period (195 µs) is about 90,000 core cycles; the demodulation below uses under 3,000.

  1. Coherent demodulation. For each period, take the 100 samples of RX (ADC A) and ITX (ADC B) and compute the five DFT bins k = 1, 2, 3, 4, 8. Form Sk = RXk / ITXk, a complex number per line that is independent of transmit amplitude and phase. Average 8–64 periods (1.5–12 ms) for the fast channel; the recovery-speed setting is this integration length.
  2. Ground model. Magnetic soil (viscous remanent magnetisation) has a response that is nearly constant in magnitude and phase across the band; salt is a conductive response that rises with frequency. With five lines, fit a two-component ground vector G = a·gmag + b·gsalt to the slowly varying part of S and subtract it; that is the multi-frequency generalisation of a published two-frequency ground-processing technique (channel 3 = |Im S(f1) − Im S(f2)|). Tracking speed is modulated by swing velocity from the LSM6DSM, following a position-aware ground-balance approach: slow when the coil is held over a target, fast when covering new ground.
  3. Target vector and 2-D ID. A conductive target's polarisability is M(ω) = −C · (jf/ζ)/(1 + jf/ζ), where ζ is the relaxation frequency. Fitting ζ and C to the five ground-balanced Sk gives a conductivity axis (ζ) and, from the sign and frequency dependence of the real part, a ferrous axis. That is the 2-D conductive/ferrous target map used by high-end detectors, computed from the same five lines.
  4. Noise cancel. Run the five DFT bins between the transmit lines as noise monitors; if a bin shows narrowband interference (another detector, mains harmonics, switching supplies), rescale the LUT period by ±1–3 % so the lines move. Because the sample count per period is fixed by the timer, coherence is preserved at any shift.
  5. Audio. The fast channel drives tone pitch/volume through DAC2 with about 4 ms latency to the headphone jack; the Bluetooth module adds codec latency and is optional.
7

Pulse-induction mode on the same bridge

Sequence

  1. Firmware enables the second LT3757, which boosts VTX (set to 24 V) to a 100 V bridge rail; 27 µF of bank capacitance stores 0.13 J.
  2. Current reversal: opposite diagonal of the bridge on, 100 V across 0.35 mH gives di/dt = 286 A/ms, so a −2 A to +2 A reversal takes 14 µs. The coil energy returns to the bank through the MOSFET body diodes; the boost supplies only losses.
  3. Hold: both low-side MOSFETs on (zero voltage across the coil, current freewheels; τ = L/R ≈ 0.6 ms). Short PWM top-ups from the rail keep the average current constant cycle to cycle, regulated from ADC B — the zero-voltage-transmission (ZVT) constant-current principle.
  4. Receive during the hold periods: the RX channel sees only target and ground decay, with the transmit field static. Sample windows from 5 µs to 200 µs after each reversal are summed in firmware for early (small gold) and late (deep, large) channels.

Protection and housekeeping

  • Two TLV3501 comparators watch the INA241 output for ±5 A and drive TIM1's break input; all four gates go off within one timer clock, independent of firmware.
  • Bridge rail and VTX are monitored by the MCU ADC through dividers; the 100 V bank is discharged through 4.7 kΩ under MCU control when leaving PI mode.
  • The receive preamp saturates at ±125 mV coil input during the reversal and clamps at VOCM ± 0.6 V; with 2 µs recovery, the earliest usable sample sits at about 5 µs, comparable to the best PI machines.
Pulse rate, reversal amplitude, hold length and sample windows are all firmware parameters. Multi-loop ground tracking and dual-channel ground-balance schemes are models of the same decay samples, so both can be reproduced and combined.

Schematics

Seven hierarchical sheets. Signals between sheets are global labels; every rail has a power symbol; unused pins carry no-connect markers. The full-resolution PDF is at docs/MDX-1_schematic.pdf. Each sheet carries design notes in its top-left corner.

9

PCB: 135 × 92 mm, 4 layers, placed by function

Stackup and layout rules to route against

  • L1 signals and components · L2 unbroken ground · L3 +3V3 plane under MCU/UI, routed rails elsewhere · L4 signals and ground pour. 1.6 mm, 1 oz outer, 0.5 oz inner.
  • RX front end (top right) is the quietest corner: 20 mm from any switching converter, its own ground island under the OPA1612 stitched to L2 at one edge, and the coil connector's RX pins routed as a coupled differential pair straight to the 47 Ω resistors.
  • TX bridge (top centre): the four MOSFETs, the 200 V ceramics and the shunt form a loop under 10 mm; the INA241 sits at the shunt with Kelvin sense traces; the bootstrap capacitors sit at the driver pins.
  • Boost converters (left) keep their switch nodes under 5 mm² and their inductors on the board edge, oriented to point their leakage away from the RX corner.
  • ADC clock and SPI run on L1 over solid ground with 33 Ω series termination; the two DRDY lines go to EXTI pins with equal length.
  • Design-rule set in the project: 0.15 mm track / 0.15 mm clearance, 0.45 mm vias with 0.2 mm drill. Open DRC items are the unrouted ratsnest (499) and two fine-pitch footprint courtyard/clearance classes that need the default netclass relaxed to 0.1 mm.

What the automatic checks do not cover

  • Configuration pins were reviewed line by line against the datasheets in rev A2 (57 checks, 13 corrections) and the whole schematic was reviewed again for rev A3 (regulator input capacitors, USB ESD, 5 V LCD rail, antenna matching, HV bleed, gauge and amplifier bypassing, 17 test points); the STM32 pin map was verified against DS12110 Tables 9 and 10. Both are documented on the review and BOM page.
  • Thermal: the LT3045 dissipates about 0.2 W dropping 12 V to 5 V; the bridge MOSFETs dissipate under 50 mW in VLF mode. No heatsinking is needed, but the 100 V boost inductor should be checked for saturation at 2.5 A.

Next steps

  1. Desk review of the schematic against datasheets for the configuration pins listed in section 10, then validate the STM32 pin map in CubeMX. Edit the generator, re-run it, and the netlist check and ERC re-run in seconds.
  2. Route both boards in KiCad from the placed files, following the rules in section 9; fill zones; clear DRC. The main board can now shrink below 135 × 92 mm since its UI zone only holds the IMU, audio and radios.
  3. Build the coil to the sheet-7 specification and null it on the bench to under 20 mV residual at the preamp input; program the DS2431 with the null vectors.
  4. Bring-up firmware in this order: rails and DAC-set VTX, TIM1 waveform on a resistive load, ADC streaming and DFT, then the coil. Measure the actual five-line spectrum and noise floor and compare with the figures here.
  5. Field firmware: ground model, target ID map, noise cancel, audio; then the PI sequence. Benchmark against a mature commercial reference detector on a test garden with buried targets at known depths, because that is the only comparison that counts.
